intro.author: Not named. Jewish tradition credits Ezra; many scholars simply call the writer 'the Chronicler,' possibly a Levite connected with the temple.
intro.written: After the return from exile, in the Persian period — many scholars suggest around 450–400 BC. 1 and 2 Chronicles were originally one book, usually placed last in the Hebrew Bible.
intro.audience: Jews who had returned from Babylon to a small, rebuilt Judah, wondering whether they were still God's people
intro.setting: The returned exiles had a modest second temple and no king. Chronicles retells Israel's story from Adam to the exile, drawing heavily on Samuel and Kings but choosing and shaping material to encourage this community.
intro.purpose: To show the returned exiles that they were the continuation of 'all Israel,' that God's promises to David still stood, and that faithful temple worship was the heart of their life together.
intro.bigIdea: God's people find their identity in his covenant with David and in wholehearted worship at his house.
